paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate objects in three dimensions from a single image. The desired output is a tightly fitting, oriented 3D box around each object. This combines identifying an object category with estimating where the object lies and which way it faces.

The approach represents an object category as a deformable cuboid containing faces and parts. Both can move relative to their anchors on the box, allowing the representation to accommodate variation within a category. Each face's appearance is modeled in coordinates that view it straight on, helping separate appearance from viewpoint. The model also handles different combinations of visible faces and shares learned weights across them.

Detection searches over box positions and rotations and scores the resulting object hypotheses. Although the model's variables are continuous, the inference procedure uses a discretized search. Experiments in indoor and outdoor settings demonstrate effectiveness, with reported improvements over the referenced leading methods for both 2D and 3D detection.
neurips-2012-3d-object-detection-and-vie.tldr: A deformable 3D cuboid model jointly detects objects and estimates their orientation from a single image.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to prepare a Deep Boltzmann Machine for learning through pretraining. Its central concern is how the hidden layers divide the work of modeling the data. The authors connect the pretraining procedure for these models to the corresponding procedure for Deep Belief Networks, using that relationship to understand what the initialization accomplishes.

For a Deep Boltzmann Machine with two hidden layers, they show that pretraining improves a variational lower bound under certain conditions. This bound provides a tractable way to assess the model's fit. The result gives a conditional theoretical justification for pretraining, while also motivating a different procedure that spreads the modeling work more evenly across hidden layers.

The authors evaluate the revised procedure on MNIST and NORB and report better generative models. The stated outcome concerns how well the learned models represent data distributions. Together, the analysis and experiments support changing the allocation of modeling work during pretraining as a way to improve these models.
neurips-2012-a-better-way-to-pretrain-de.tldr: A revised pretraining method distributes modeling work more evenly across hidden layers and improves generative results on MNIST and NORB.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a classification criterion focused on the highest scores produced by a model. A parameter specifies the upper fraction of scores that matters. This captures a concern arising in search engines: the quality of the items placed near the top deserves its own learning objective.

To make that objective tractable, the authors optimize a convex surrogate for the associated loss. A surrogate is an alternative objective used to guide learning when directly optimizing the desired criterion is difficult. They show that obtaining their algorithm's solution can be organized into several convex optimization problems. They also establish margin-based guarantees that incorporate the relevant score quantile of candidate functions.

Experiments evaluate the resulting algorithm, including comparisons with several methods designed for high precision at the top in a bipartite setting. The proposed method achieves better top precision in that comparison. The contribution therefore combines an explicit target for learning, an optimization procedure, and theoretical support tied to the same upper portion of the ranking.
neurips-2012-accuracy-at-the-top-65494c1.tldr: The paper develops a learning objective and algorithm for classification accuracy among the highest-scoring items.

paragraphs: Adaptive generalized approximate message passing addresses recovery of an unknown vector when the statistical assumptions needed for recovery must also be learned. Measurements arise from a known linear transformation followed by a probabilistic channel acting on individual components, which may be nonlinear. The unknown vector's entries are assumed to be independent and identically distributed.

The algorithm jointly estimates the vector and learns parameters describing its prior and the measurement channel. It extends an earlier approach that combines expectation-maximization with approximate message passing. This makes the framework applicable to problems such as learning sparse priors in compressed sensing and identifying linear–nonlinear models of dynamical systems or neural spiking.

For large transformation matrices with independent, identically distributed Gaussian entries, the authors prove that scalar state-evolution equations describe asymptotic componentwise behavior. Their analysis shows that parameter estimates can be asymptotically consistent. In that setting, reconstruction can match an oracle that already knows the correct parameters, giving conditional theoretical support for learning those parameters during recovery.
neurips-2012-approximate-message-passing.tldr: Adaptive GAMP jointly learns unknown statistical parameters and reconstructs signals, with asymptotic guarantees for large Gaussian transformation matrices.

paragraphs: Sequential auctions create linked decisions: the desirability of an outcome in one auction can depend on what happens in others. Bidders also have limited knowledge of competitors' preferences and past actions. These dependencies make it difficult to reason directly about bidding strategies, especially when bidders want multiple units.

The paper organizes the bidder's problem around learning price predictions and optimizing decisions using them. It introduces stable price predictions and connects them to equilibrium. More precisely, an approximate equilibrium can be characterized through strategies that approximately optimize against approximately stable predictions. Keeping those approximations explicit matters because the framework addresses settings where exact strategic solutions are difficult to obtain.

The authors compare equilibria obtained through this formulation with theoretical equilibria already known for simpler auction settings. They also find new approximate equilibria in a more complex domain for which analytical solutions had been unknown. The contribution is a way to turn interdependent strategic reasoning into linked prediction and optimization problems while retaining a connection to equilibrium.
neurips-2012-approximating-equilibria-in.tldr: Stable price predictions connect learning and optimization to approximate equilibrium in complex sequential auctions.

paragraphs: This paper extends the Plackett–Luce choice model to ranked data with an infinite collection of possible items. The distinction concerns the space of available choices: the model can accommodate an unbounded item universe while describing observed rankings. This gives ranked-data modeling a Bayesian nonparametric formulation.

The mathematical construction uses random atomic measures, with a gamma process specifying the prior. These measures provide a way to associate statistical weight with individual items. The authors derive a characterization of the posterior, describing how the model changes after rankings are observed, and develop a Gibbs sampler for drawing from that posterior. The inference procedure makes the proposed model usable for posterior simulation.

The authors also extend the model so that it can vary over time and apply it to weekly New York Times bestseller lists. This application brings together ranking and temporal change within one framework. The stated contribution consists of the expanded choice model, its posterior analysis, a sampling method, and a time-varying version demonstrated on ranked book data.
neurips-2012-bayesian-nonparametric-mode.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric extension of Plackett–Luce models rankings over infinitely many possible items and supports temporal variation.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much computation an approximate Bayesian decision maker should perform before acting. Exact inference is generally intractable in complex models, so additional computation trades time for accuracy. The authors use Metropolis–Hastings sampling as a metaphor for mental inference to study that tradeoff.

They find that decisions can become reasonably accurate before the sampling chain has converged to the posterior distribution. During this initial period, called burn-in, samples still depend on the starting value. With limited processing speed and costs for spending more time, an optimal strategy may stop after relatively few iterations. Its estimates can therefore remain pulled toward their initial value.

This mechanism provides a rational account of anchoring and adjustment: an initial estimate continues to influence the final judgment because further computation may not justify its cost. The authors test quantitative predictions against published numerical-estimation data. Their theoretical and empirical results suggest that anchoring is consistent with approximate Bayesian inference, using the sampling model as an explanatory account of the behavior.
neurips-2012-burn-in-bias-and-the-ration.tldr: Anchoring may reflect a rational decision to stop approximate Bayesian computation before its dependence on the initial estimate disappears.

paragraphs: Neural signals take time to transmit and process, creating a challenge for tracking moving stimuli as they change. This paper studies how the dynamics of synapses can help a continuous attractor network compensate for those delays. The relevant synaptic mechanism is short-term depression, a temporary reduction in synaptic effectiveness.

The authors show that this mechanism can make the network's activity state sufficiently mobile to track a stimulus without lag or even lead it by an effectively constant time. Different parameter regions support delayed, zero-lag, and anticipatory tracking. These correspond respectively to network states that are static, poised to move, or moving spontaneously, linking tracking behavior to the network's intrinsic dynamics.

The zero-lag and anticipatory behaviors agree with experiments on rodent head-direction systems. The authors also identify a specific condition under which delay becomes effectively independent of stimulus amplitude: the stimulus moves at the network state's natural speed. These findings explain how timely tracking can emerge from internal dynamics, with performance depending on the network's operating regime.
neurips-2012-delay-compensation-with-dyn.tldr: Short-term synaptic depression can enable a neural network to track moving stimuli without lag or anticipate their position.

paragraphs: GenDeR addresses how to produce a top-k list that balances relevance with diversity. The setting accepts an arbitrary relevance function and an arbitrary similarity function between examples. This separates the ranking method from any one definition of relevance or similarity, making the formulation applicable across tasks such as retrieval, product search, and team assembly.

The authors express diversified ranking as an optimization problem and show that the general problem is NP-hard. They also identify useful structure across a large portion of the parameter space: the objective has diminishing returns. In practical terms, the additional value of selecting an item can decrease as the selected collection grows. This property supports a scalable greedy procedure with a near-optimal solution.

Experiments on real datasets demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness. The theoretical qualification matters: the stated diminishing-returns structure holds over a substantial parameter region, rather than being asserted for every setting. The paper's contribution is to connect a flexible ranking objective to a computationally manageable method where that structure applies.
neurips-2012-gender-a-generic-diversifie.tldr: GenDeR uses diminishing-returns structure in a broad parameter region to build diverse, relevant rankings with a scalable greedy algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper tackles two related ways of simplifying supervised learning inputs. Feature extraction creates a small number of new features from the original predictors, while variable selection retains a subset of those predictors. Both aim to preserve useful predictive information in a reduced representation.

The proposed kernel method uses the gradient of a regression function to construct linear features. A gradient describes how the function changes as its inputs change, making it relevant to identifying informative directions. The resulting procedure uses eigendecomposition, which the authors describe as computationally simple and applicable to large datasets. They also emphasize broad applicability without strong assumptions about the regression function or variable types.

Adding a sparsity penalty extends the approach to variable selection. This encourages a solution that depends on fewer predictors, connecting the extraction method to selecting original inputs. Experiments show that the methods identify effective features and variables without parametric models. The contribution is a shared gradient-based framework for these two forms of dimension reduction.
neurips-2012-gradient-based-kernel-metho.tldr: A kernel method uses regression gradients to extract informative features and, with a sparsity penalty, select useful variables.

paragraphs: HORSE.C gives a mathematical formulation to a particular curiosity-driven learning problem. A continuous space is divided into a fixed, supplied partition, and an unknown process is defined over that space. At each step, the learner must choose both a region and a location within that region at which to sample.

The objective assigns each region a loss with two components. One measures a worst-case quadratic sampling error, and the other penalizes the range of variance within the region. This makes the sampling goal explicit: decisions should improve performance according to that specified combination of error and variability. The formulation extends active learning for multi-armed bandits by treating each arm as a continuous region.

The proposed procedure combines adaptations of active-learning bandit algorithms with hierarchical optimistic sampling methods used in optimization. The authors provide a finite-time regret analysis for the resulting algorithm. Its significance is a theoretically analyzed sampling rule for this defined curiosity objective, tying the motivation for exploration to measurable performance over a finite period.
neurips-2012-hierarchical-optimistic-reg.tldr: HORSE.C formalizes curiosity-driven sampling across continuous regions and provides a hierarchical algorithm with finite-time regret analysis.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether neuroimaging measurements can predict how cognitive performance changes over time in Alzheimer's disease research. Relating an image to cognitive status at one point is only part of that problem. Predicting a trajectory requires accounting for relationships among measurements and prediction tasks across time.

The authors propose a high-order multi-task learning model that uses structured sparsity-inducing norms to capture those temporal correlations. Such penalties encourage selective use of features while respecting relationships represented in the learning problem. By linking the regression tasks, the method uses their temporal structure as part of how it learns predictions.

Sparsity also allows the model to select a small collection of MRI measures while maintaining high prediction accuracy. The empirical study uses baseline MRI measurements and repeated cognitive observations from the ADNI cohort and reports promising results. The stated contribution is a structured prediction method that combines trajectory modeling with selection of a compact set of imaging measures relevant to the prediction task.
neurips-2012-high-order-multi-task-featu.tldr: A structured multi-task model uses baseline MRI measures to predict cognitive trajectories while selecting a small set of imaging features.

paragraphs: This paper seeks to learn the balance between speed and accuracy in natural language processing automatically. It focuses on agenda-based syntactic parsing, where prioritizing pending work affects both computation and the quality of the resulting analysis. The goal is to learn priorities using only a few inexpensive features.

The authors report that standard reinforcement learning performs poorly because the state space is too large for naive exploration. Imitation learning also fails in their setting: the teacher's behavior is too demanding to reproduce with the cheap features available to the learner. In addition, the teacher is not specifically optimized for the known reward function that expresses the desired tradeoff.

Their solution combines reinforcement learning with apprenticeship learning. This hybrid learns feature weights that achieve competitive parsing accuracy while substantially improving speed relative to the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. The finding supports learning a prioritization policy that fits both the available information and the computational objective, rather than assuming that direct exploration or teacher imitation alone will suffice.
neurips-2012-learned-prioritization-for-.tldr: A hybrid reinforcement and apprenticeship learning method learns parsing priorities that substantially improve speed while retaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper formulates binary classification as a discrete optimization problem. Learning becomes the search for a maximum a posteriori, or MAP, configuration in a graphical model. Its potential functions are low-dimensional discrete substitutes for misclassification loss, so the classification objective is represented through interacting discrete choices.

This reduction allows guarantees from applicable MAP inference settings to carry over to learning. The formulation remains nonconvex, but its discrete structure gives access to tools and guarantees associated with graphical-model inference. Experiments show promise in settings including severe label noise, while retaining global optimality guarantees in the settings considered.

The discrete representation also permits direct penalties on the number of selected features, including the l0 pseudo-norm. This makes feature selection part of the learning objective and provides a principled way to balance interpretability with predictive performance. The paper presents this formulation as a broader route to classification and identifies open problems arising from it, combining empirical evidence with guarantees inherited from suitable inference problems.
neurips-2012-learning-as-map-inference-i.tldr: Binary classification is reformulated as discrete MAP inference, enabling applicable inference guarantees and direct feature-count penalties.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to define wavelets for signals on permutations. Permutations describe different arrangements of a collection, and the symmetric group contains all such arrangements. A multiresolution representation aims to organize information at different levels of detail, but the authors note that no generally accepted wavelet construction existed for this setting.

Their construction is called coset-based multiresolution analysis. It uses the structure of the symmetric group to define the resolution hierarchy and derives corresponding wavelet functions. The authors also describe a fast transform for sparse signals with complexity O(n^p), where p is small. The sparsity qualification is part of this computational claim.

That complexity contrasts with the O(n^q n!) cost the abstract associates with typical fast Fourier transforms in this setting. Removing the factorial factor for the stated sparse-signal case is the key computational attraction. Ranking, sparse approximation, and multi-object tracking are discussed as potential applications, giving possible uses for the representation beyond the mathematical construction itself.
neurips-2012-multiresolution-analysis-on.tldr: Coset-based multiresolution analysis defines wavelets on permutations and supports a polynomial-time transform for sparse signals.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a Gaussian process model for data that combine long-range dependence with abrupt changes. These two properties need distinct treatment within the representation: observations far apart can remain related, while local transitions can be sudden. The model accommodates both through a hierarchy of coupled smooth Gaussian processes.

Each process is defined on one element of a random nested partition. The process at the top of the hierarchy captures long-range dependencies, while partition boundaries determine where abrupt changes occur. The partition therefore has a direct modeling role: inferring its structure helps identify how the data divide into regions within the multiresolution description.

Gaussian-process conjugacy allows the authors to integrate out the processes analytically and compute the observations' conditional likelihood given the partition tree. This supports efficient inference over the partition itself using graph-theoretic techniques. The model is applied to magnetoencephalography recordings of brain activity, illustrating a setting in which the combined treatment of long-range relationships and sudden changes can be used.
neurips-2012-multiresolution-gaussian-pr.tldr: Hierarchically coupled Gaussian processes model long-range dependencies and abrupt changes through an inferred nested partition.

paragraphs: The paper develops a nonparametric approach to approximate dynamic programming. A central design challenge in parametric approaches is specifying an approximation architecture carefully enough to represent the decision problem well. The proposed method aims to reduce that burden by using a kernel-based formulation.

The authors construct a mathematical optimization program for approximate dynamic programming and establish approximation and sample-complexity guarantees that are independent of dimension. These guarantees concern the quality of approximation and the samples required by the proposal. They provide theoretical support for treating the kernel method as a viable alternative to established parametric approaches.

A computational study on a controlled queueing network supplies the empirical comparison. In that study, the nonparametric method is competitive with parametric approximate dynamic programming. The stated result supports the possibility of obtaining useful performance without requiring the designer to carefully prescribe an approximation architecture. The theoretical guarantees and computational evidence address complementary parts of that case: what can be established about the method and how it performs in the studied control problem.
neurips-2012-non-parametric-approximate-.tldr: A kernel-based approximate dynamic programming method offers dimension-independent guarantees and competitive results on a controlled queueing network.

paragraphs: This paper models structure in how many variables receive a particular label. In an image, the number of objects can carry information; in search, the number of highly relevant documents can do the same. The proposed framework makes such counts an explicit part of a probabilistic model.

It combines a prior distribution over counts with a likelihood over subsets of a specified size. The count describes how many items receive a label, while the conditional likelihood describes which items they are. With binary labels and a Poisson–Binomial count prior, the formulation recovers standard logistic regression. Other count distributions introduce dependencies across labels.

Those dependencies create apparent combinatorial difficulties because possible subsets must be accounted for. The authors nevertheless derive simple, efficient learning procedures for more general versions of the model. Applications to multi-object classification, learning to rank, and top-K classification illustrate its utility. The contribution is a way to include knowledge about label totals while retaining practical learning procedures beyond the logistic-regression special case.
neurips-2012-probabilistic-n-choose-k-mo.tldr: Probabilistic count priors extend classification and ranking models to capture dependencies in how many items receive each label.

paragraphs: The paper changes the objective of a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem to account for risk. Standard formulations seek high expected reward while balancing exploration with exploitation. Here, the learner instead competes with the arm offering the best balance between return and risk, using variance as the measure of risk.

This objective makes exploration more complicated. The authors identify an exploration risk that produces regret associated with the algorithm's own variability. Thus, evaluating a learning strategy requires accounting for the risk introduced by its behavior during learning as well as the risk–return qualities of the available arms. The resulting setting is intrinsically harder than the standard bandit problem.

The authors introduce two algorithms for this formulation and investigate their theoretical guarantees. They also report preliminary empirical results. The contribution is both a new decision criterion and methods for pursuing it, with analysis showing why a concern for variability changes the learning problem. The empirical evidence is presented as preliminary support alongside that theoretical investigation.
neurips-2012-risk-aversion-in-multi-arme.tldr: A variance-based risk-averse bandit formulation exposes additional exploration risk and motivates two new learning algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper presents a Bayesian nonparametric model for collections of genetic sequences. It describes the sequences through partitions that change along the genome. At each location, a partition groups sequences into clusters, and a Markov model connects the grouping at one location to the next.

The transition works through two stages: existing clusters split, and the resulting clusters then merge. This creates a discrete-time counterpart to a previously developed continuous-time fragmentation–coagulation process. The construction preserves projectivity, exchangeability, and reversibility while improving scalability. These are structural properties of the probabilistic model that the authors retain as they change how its transitions are represented.

The authors apply the model to genotype imputation, the task of filling in missing genetic data. They report better computational efficiency while maintaining the accuracy of the earlier continuous-time approach. The finding therefore supports a computational advantage for the discrete formulation in the studied application, with the model's important probabilistic properties preserved and no reported loss in imputation accuracy.
neurips-2012-scalable-imputation-of-gene.tldr: A discrete split-and-merge model improves genetic imputation efficiency while preserving the earlier model's accuracy and key probabilistic properties.

paragraphs: The paper develops optimization methods for large problems whose objectives are both nonsmooth and nonconvex. It focuses on composite objectives, which combine multiple terms within one optimization problem. The framework also includes convex composite problems as a special case, placing familiar settings within a broader formulation.

A central feature is its treatment of computational errors that do not disappear asymptotically. Many analyses assume that errors eventually vanish; this framework explicitly accommodates persistent errors. That changes the conditions under which the authors develop and analyze proximal splitting methods, which organize optimization around the components of the objective.

Within the framework, the authors derive both batch and incremental algorithms. They identify the development and analysis of incremental nonconvex proximal splitting as novel to their knowledge, even apart from the treatment of nonvanishing errors. Applications to difficult large-scale, nonsmooth, nonconvex problems illustrate the framework. The contribution is an expanded analytical and algorithmic foundation for composite optimization under persistent inexactness, together with two styles of algorithm.
neurips-2012-scalable-nonconvex-inexact-.tldr: A proximal splitting framework handles nonconvex composite objectives with persistent computational errors and yields batch and incremental algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses data analysis focused on a particular region of a large dataset. A user may have labels or other information identifying that region and want learning to concentrate nearby. Standard eigenvector-based methods are challenging to use for this purpose because eigenvectors describe global structure.

The authors construct semi-supervised eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian using a supplied seed set of nodes. These vectors capture directions of maximum variance while being constrained to correlate well with the seeds. Successive directions are orthogonalized, providing distinct directions that retain the intended local emphasis. The seed set is therefore an essential input linking the mathematical representation to the region of interest.

Several empirical examples demonstrate how the resulting vectors support locally biased learning. The contribution is a way to incorporate partial supervision into eigenvector construction itself, so that the representation reflects the target region. This connects a global analysis tool to tasks in which the relevant structure is defined partly by what the user already knows.
neurips-2012-semi-supervised-eigenvector.tldr: Semi-supervised graph eigenvectors use seed nodes to focus variance-based representations on a chosen region of a dataset.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to cluster a collection of hidden Markov models according to the probability distributions they represent. The objects being grouped are themselves probabilistic models. Similarity is therefore defined through their distributions, giving the clustering a direct connection to the behavior each model describes.

The proposed variational hierarchical expectation-maximization algorithm has two linked outputs. It groups HMMs with similar distributions and constructs a new representative HMM for each group. This representative acts as a cluster center, expressing the group's shared structure in the same model form as its members. The method thus produces both an organization of the collection and probabilistic summaries of its groups.

The authors illustrate benefits in hierarchical clustering of motion-capture sequences and in automatic music tagging. These applications demonstrate how clustering HMMs can support analysis of sequence-related data. The central contribution is the combination of distribution-based grouping with learned HMM representatives, allowing the cluster summaries to remain explicit models rather than only group assignments.
neurips-2012-the-variational-hierarchica.tldr: A variational hierarchical EM algorithm groups HMMs by their distributions and learns a representative HMM for each cluster.

paragraphs: This paper improves online inference for a topic model based on the hierarchical Dirichlet process. Variational methods offer scalable approximate Bayesian learning, but conventional batch and online versions can quickly become trapped in local optima. For a nonparametric topic model, that can interfere with its ability to keep adapting its topic structure.

The authors derive a simpler, faster variational approximation and add updates that split and merge components of the approximate posterior. These operations allow the algorithm to revise how topics are organized during learning. They report substantially better predictions on test data than conventional online and batch variational algorithms.

The streaming setting is especially relevant because large datasets can make batch analysis infeasible. The authors show that split-and-merge updates better preserve the underlying model's nonparametric behavior, enabling continued learning of new topics. The contribution connects scalable inference with structural adaptation: processing more data can also change the collection of topics used to explain it, rather than merely refining an already settled organization.
neurips-2012-truly-nonparametric-online-.tldr: Split-and-merge updates improve online variational HDP inference and allow continued discovery of topics in streaming data.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an object representation based on curvature self-similarity, extending representations that approximate objects with straight lines. Its goal is to provide informative features for category-level detection. Comparing curvature structure produces a rich descriptor, but its second-order statistics also create a high-dimensional representation.

That dimensionality introduces a learning problem when training data are limited. Noisy or redundant dimensions can impair generalization, and the authors argue that even sophisticated kernel methods cannot adequately suppress them in this setting. They therefore pair the representation with feature selection embedded in support vector machine learning. The selection method reduces model complexity and improves generalization capability.

The authors integrate both the curvature descriptor and the feature-selection method into an established object detection framework, demonstrating the approach's relevance. The contribution combines a more informative representation with a learning mechanism suited to its dimensionality. The result emphasizes that adding descriptive detail and selecting useful dimensions are connected parts of building an effective object model under limited training data.
neurips-2012-visual-recognition-using-em.tldr: Curvature self-similarity features are paired with embedded SVM feature selection to reduce complexity and improve object-model generalization.
